domain_entities.name: LeaveRequest
attributes: reversesRequestId: string | null  // NEW — null for every ordinary request; set only on a reversal instance, referencing the APPROVED row it reverses
domain_entities.purpose: The canonical leave application entity, extended with a self-referencing reversal link so that a completed approval can be reversed by a NEW instance instead of being mutated (GP-008). One row = one immutable decision record; a reversal is a second row pointing back at the first.
lifecycle_states: REVERSED (derived: status=APPROVED and a reversal instance references this id)

domain_entities.name: LeaveReversal
attributes: id: string  // new identity, distinct from the original
reversesRequestId: string  // non-null; the id of the APPROVED original
employeeId: string  // copied from the original
leaveTypeCode: LeaveTypeCode  // copied from the original
startDate: Date  // copied from the original
endDate: Date  // copied from the original
requestedDays: number  // copied verbatim from the original, never re-derived
reason: string | null  // copied from the original
approverId: null  // a reversal is never approved
cancelledBy: string  // the actor who performed the reversal
domain_entities.purpose: The domain concept of a reversal: a distinct LeaveRequest instance created when an APPROVED request is cancelled. It is the only legal way to undo a completed approval; it never mutates the original. Realized as a leave_requests row with reversesRequestId set (persistence is the data architect's concern).
lifecycle_states: CANCELLED_BY_REVERSAL (created directly in this state; no prior state)

domain_entities.name: LeaveBalance
domain_entities.purpose: The per-employee, per-leave-type, per-accrual-period reservation ledger. Shape is unchanged by this feature; only the release semantics on reversal are pinned (exactly one release, in the reversal's transaction).
lifecycle_states: CLOSED (derived: current date at or after periodEnd)

domain_entities.name: AuditLog
attributes: action: AuditAction  // CANCEL for both in-place cancellation and reversal
entityId: string  // the reversal instance id for a reversal; the mutated row id for an in-place cancellation
beforeState: unknown | null  // the original APPROVED row for a reversal
afterState: unknown | null  // the reversal instance (carries reversesRequestId)
domain_entities.purpose: The immutable record of a state-changing operation (GP-002). A reversal writes exactly one CANCEL record, attributed to the reversal instance, with the original APPROVED row as beforeState.

domain_entities.name: Notification
attributes: recipientId: string  // the original request's employeeId
relatedEntityId: string | null  // the reversal instance id
domain_entities.purpose: The requester-facing notice emitted once per cancellation. Unchanged in shape; a reversal emits exactly one notice pointing at the reversal instance.

business_rules: A completed approval is immutable. Once a LeaveRequest reaches APPROVED, its status, approverId, approvalComment and decidedAt must never be written again by any operation. Reversing an approval creates a NEW LeaveRequest instance (status CANCELLED, reversesRequestId = original.id) and leaves the original row byte-identical. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveRequest completed-approval immutability (GP-008) appears, not only here]

Cancellation has exactly two modes, selected by the target's status: (a) IN-PLACE — target is DRAFT or SUBMITTED: the same row transitions to CANCELLED with cancelledBy/cancelledAt set and reversesRequestId stays null; (b) REVERSAL — target is APPROVED: a new row is inserted with status CANCELLED, reversesRequestId = target.id, cancelledBy/cancelledAt set, and the target row is not written at all. No other status may be cancelled. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveRequest cancellation mode selection appears, not only here]

A reversal instance copies employeeId, leaveTypeCode, startDate, endDate, requestedDays and reason verbatim from the original. requestedDays is never re-derived on the reversal — it is the same canonical inclusive count (endDate - startDate + 1) already persisted on the original, so the released amount and the reserved amount are provably equal. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever requestedDays day-count derivation appears, not only here]

Balance release happens exactly once per cancellation, in the same transaction as the cancellation write, and the amount is the full requestedDays with no pro-rating: DRAFT releases nothing (no balance read or write); SUBMITTED decrements pendingDays by requestedDays; APPROVED (reversal) decrements usedDays by requestedDays. A reversal must not double-release (the original approval's usedDays increment is undone once) and must not skip the release. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveBalance release on cancellation/reversal appears, not only here]

A reversal instance is terminal and inert: it is created directly in CANCELLED, is never submitted, approved, rejected or cancelled again, and never reserves or releases balance. It exists solely as the immutable record that the original approval was undone. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveReversal lifecycle appears, not only here]

A reversal is authorized by exactly the same rule as an APPROVED cancellation today: the requester's direct manager (employee.managerId === actor.id) or an ADMIN; the owner may not reverse their own APPROVED request. The timing guard is unchanged: reversal is blocked once startDate <= today (UTC day comparison) with ConflictError, which is what makes the full, non-pro-rated release correct. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveRequest reversal authorization and timing appears, not only here]

Every cancellation writes exactly one AuditLog with action CANCEL. For an in-place cancellation entityId is the mutated row and beforeState/afterState are that row before/after. For a reversal entityId is the NEW reversal instance id, beforeState is the original APPROVED row, and afterState is the reversal instance (so the audit trail shows the original was not mutated). [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever AuditLog for cancellation/reversal (GP-002) appears, not only here]

The read model must expose reversesRequestId on every LeaveRequest returned by list and single-read, so a client can distinguish the two rows that now represent a cancelled-after-approval request: the original (status APPROVED, reversesRequestId null) and the reversal (status CANCELLED, reversesRequestId = original.id). A client must never have to infer the pairing from matching dates or employee. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveRequest read model / wire contract appears, not only here]

A reversal instance is an ordinary LeaveRequest for visibility purposes: it is owned by the same employeeId as the original, so the existing role-scoped visibility (EMPLOYEE own, MANAGER own + direct reports, ADMIN all) applies unchanged, and the not-visible 404-equivalence rule applies unchanged. Reversal rows are not hidden from list results. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveRequest visibility scoping appears, not only here]

reversesRequestId is nullable and, when set, must reference an existing LeaveRequest whose status is APPROVED and whose id differs from the referencing row's own id. At most one reversal instance may reference a given original (a second reversal of the same approval is a ConflictError). [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveRequest.reversesRequestId referential integrity appears, not only here]

The original APPROVED row's "reversed" condition is DERIVED, never stored: a request is reversed iff some LeaveRequest has reversesRequestId = its id. No REVERSED status value is added to LeaveStatus and the original's status stays APPROVED forever. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever LeaveStatus enum and reversal derivation appears, not only here]

The reversal insert, the balance release, the CANCEL audit record and the cancellation notification are one atomic unit of work: all four succeed or none do. The reversal instance is never persisted without its audit record and its single balance release. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever Cancellation/reversal transaction boundary appears, not only here]
domain_notes:
## Domain slice — GP-008: an approved leave request is reversed, not mutated

### Entities and attributes
- **LeaveRequest** (15 fields): id, employeeId, leaveTypeCode, startDate, endDate, requestedDays, reason, status, approverId, approvalComment, submittedAt, decidedAt, cancelledBy, cancelledAt, **reversesRequestId: string | null** (NEW). `CreateLeaveRequestInput` remains `Omit<LeaveRequest, 'id'>`; every ordinary create supplies `reversesRequestId: null`.
- **LeaveReversal** — the domain concept realized as a LeaveRequest row with `reversesRequestId` set. Created directly in CANCELLED; copies employeeId, leaveTypeCode, startDate, endDate, requestedDays, reason verbatim; approverId/approvalComment/submittedAt/decidedAt all null; cancelledBy/cancelledAt set.
- **LeaveBalance**, **AuditLog**, **Notification** — shapes unchanged; only their reversal-time semantics are pinned.

### Lifecycle states (all must be folded into architectureMdUpdate)
Stored states (unchanged enum `LeaveStatus`): **DRAFT, SUBMITTED, APPROVED, REJECTED, CANCELLED**. No new enum member is added — `REVERSED` is deliberately NOT a status.
Derived states introduced by this feature (must be named in the architecture doc):
- **CANCELLED_IN_PLACE** — `status = CANCELLED` and `reversesRequestId = null` (DRAFT/SUBMITTED cancelled in place).
- **CANCELLED_BY_REVERSAL** — `status = CANCELLED` and `reversesRequestId != null` (the reversal instance).
- **REVERSED** — `status = APPROVED` and some LeaveRequest has `reversesRequestId = this.id`. Derived, never stored; the original's status stays APPROVED forever.
LeaveBalance: OPEN, CLOSED (derived from period vs now). AuditLog: RECORDED. Notification: PENDING, SENT, READ, ARCHIVED.

### Named transitions
- `cancelInPlace`: DRAFT → CANCELLED (same row; no balance touch); SUBMITTED → CANCELLED (same row; pendingDays -= requestedDays).
- `reverseApproval`: APPROVED → REVERSED (original row untouched) **plus** creation of a new row in CANCELLED_BY_REVERSAL (usedDays -= requestedDays).
- `createReversalInstance`: (none) → CANCELLED_BY_REVERSAL, terminal.
- All other transitions (submit, approve, reject) unchanged.

### Business rules (all scope "broad")
1. Completed approval immutability (GP-008): status/approverId/approvalComment/decidedAt of an APPROVED row are never written again.
2. Two cancellation modes selected by target status; no other status cancellable.
3. Reversal copies requestedDays verbatim — never re-derived; the canonical inclusive count `endDate - startDate + 1` (whole UTC calendar days, no weekend/holiday exclusion) remains the single derivation, and the reversal reuses the already-persisted value so released == reserved.
4. Balance release exactly once, in the same transaction, full requestedDays, no pro-rating (DRAFT: none; SUBMITTED: pendingDays; APPROVED: usedDays).
5. Reversal instance is terminal and inert.
6. Reversal authorization = direct manager or ADMIN (owner may not reverse own APPROVED); timing guard `startDate <= today` (UTC) → ConflictError.
7. Exactly one AuditLog per cancellation; for a reversal entityId = the new instance, beforeState = the original APPROVED row.
8. Read model exposes `reversesRequestId` on every LeaveRequest (list and single-read) so the two rows are distinguishable.
9. Reversal rows obey existing role-scoped visibility and 404-equivalence unchanged.
10. `reversesRequestId` nullable; when set must reference an existing APPROVED request with a different id; at most one reversal per original (second attempt → ConflictError).
11. "Reversed" is derived, never stored; no REVERSED status value.
12. Reversal insert + balance release + CANCEL audit + notification are one atomic unit of work.

### Boundary semantics made explicit (BR-001 anti-pattern avoided)
The day-count boundary is decided once, broadly, and applies to the reversal path as well as the sufficiency/deduction paths: `requestedDays = endDate - startDate + 1`, inclusive calendar days, whole-day UTC, no business-day or holiday exclusion. The reversal does not recompute it — it copies the persisted value — so the release path and the reservation path cannot diverge.

### Open questions (for the chief architect)
- Reuse `AuditAction.CANCEL` vs add `AuditAction.REVERSE` (or a distinct audit entityType).
- Whether `GET /leaves` should filter reversal rows (default both rows vs `excludeReversals`/`includeReversals` flag).
- Whether to expose a derived `isReversed` (or nested `reversedBy`) on the original APPROVED row in addition to `reversesRequestId` on the reversal.

### Out of scope for this slice
SQL DDL, the `reverses_request_id` column/index/migration, repository method signatures, service/module wiring, and route/query-param shapes — owned by the data and application architects. The domain requires only: a nullable self-reference on LeaveRequest, an index supporting lookup by it, and its presence on the read model.

open_questions.question: Should the reversal instance reuse AuditAction.CANCEL, or should a distinct AuditAction.REVERSE member be added so the audit trail distinguishes an in-place cancellation from a reversal of a completed approval?
open_questions.impact: Audit consumers (and any future reporting on how often approvals are undone) cannot tell a reversal from an ordinary cancellation without joining on reversesRequestId. Adding an enum member is a shared-types change with a migration-free but contract-visible effect.
candidate_options: Reuse AuditAction.CANCEL for both modes (current design; pairing recoverable from afterState.reversesRequestId)
Add AuditAction.REVERSE and use it only for reversal instances
Reuse CANCEL but add a dedicated audit entityType such as 'leave_request_reversal'

open_questions.question: Should GET /leaves return reversal instances by default, and should it offer a filter (e.g. excludeReversals, or filter by reversesRequestId) so a client can request only the "live" view of a request?
open_questions.impact: A cancelled-after-approval request now yields two rows in every list. Without a filter, clients that render a request list must de-duplicate or annotate client-side, and any count/aggregate over list results silently double-counts the request.
candidate_options: Return both rows unfiltered; client pairs them via reversesRequestId (current design)
Return both rows by default plus an optional excludeReversals=true query flag
Hide reversal rows from list by default and expose them only via an explicit includeReversals=true flag

open_questions.question: Should the read model expose a derived boolean (e.g. isReversed) on the original APPROVED row, in addition to reversesRequestId on the reversal row?
open_questions.impact: Without it, a client reading a single APPROVED request cannot tell it has been reversed without a second query or a scan of the list. Adding it requires the read path to resolve the reversal link, which is a query-shape decision for the application/data architects.
candidate_options: Expose only reversesRequestId on the reversal row; the original stays a plain APPROVED row (current design)
Also expose isReversed: boolean on the original, resolved by the read path
Expose a nested reversedBy: { id, cancelledAt, cancelledBy } object on the original
